meta.title: Property, plant and equipment: acquisition
meta.summary: Measuring the cost of equipment, land and buildings, self-constructed assets and interest capitalization, lump-sum purchases and other acquisitions, nonmonetary exchanges, and costs after acquisition.

videos.title: The cost of equipment
videos.take: Capitalize every cost needed to get the asset ready for its intended use

scenes.say: Bluestem buys a new paddle-molding machine. The invoice says $250,000. The asset will cost more than that on the books.

sub: not held for sale, lasting over a year
scenes.say: Property, plant and equipment are tangible assets acquired for use in operations, not for resale, with lives longer than a year: land, buildings, machinery, vehicles.

scenes.heading: Capitalized cost of the machine
scenes.say: Historical cost includes everything needed to acquire the asset and get it ready for its intended use: the $250,000 price, $6,000 of freight and transit insurance, $14,000 of installation and $5,000 of test runs. The machine costs $275,000.
Watch out: a $3,000 repair because the installers dropped a part isn't necessary to get the machine ready. It's an expense. So are training and later operating costs.
PP&E is recorded at historical cost because it's verifiable, and under US GAAP it isn't revalued upward later.

scenes.q: Which cost is NOT added to a machine's cost?
scenes.say: Quick check. Which cost is not added to a machine's cost? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, operator training: it's expensed.

videos.title: Land and buildings
videos.take: Land includes costs to prepare it for use; land improvements with limited lives are separate and depreciated

scenes.say: Bluestem buys a lot next to its plant, with an old shed on it, for a new warehouse.

scenes.heading: Cost of the land
scenes.say: Land includes the price, legal and title costs, and costs to get the land ready: demolishing the old shed, net of $5,000 of salvage, and grading. Land costs $445,000. It isn't depreciated.

scenes.heading: Land vs land improvements
scenes.say: A parking lot, fencing and lighting are land improvements: they wear out, so they're recorded separately, $60,000 here, and depreciated.

scenes.heading: Building cost
scenes.say: A building's cost includes materials, labor and overhead, architect and permit fees, excavation for the foundation, and, as we'll see next, interest during construction.

scenes.big: Buying a building to tear down
scenes.say: If a company buys land with a building it intends to tear down, the whole price, plus demolition less salvage, goes to land.
Quick check. Which of these is depreciated? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's C, the parking lot, a land improvement.

videos.title: Self-constructed assets and capitalized interest
videos.take: Capitalize avoidable interest: weighted-average expenditures times the appropriate rates, capped at actual interest

scenes.say: Bluestem builds the warehouse itself over 2027. Interest on borrowed money is part of its cost.

sub: Interest that would have been avoided
if the asset hadn't been built
scenes.say: GAAP capitalizes avoidable interest: the interest Bluestem would have avoided if it hadn't spent money on construction. It's capitalized only during construction and only for qualifying assets, not routine inventory.

scenes.heading: Weighted-average accumulated expenditures
scenes.say: Weight each payment by how long it was outstanding during the year. $300,000 paid January 1 counts in full; $600,000 paid April 1 counts for nine months, and $400,000 paid October 1 for three. Weighted-average expenditures are $850,000.

scenes.heading: Avoidable vs actual interest
scenes.say: The first $500,000 is financed by an eight percent construction loan: $40,000. The other $350,000 uses the ten percent rate on Bluestem's other debt: $35,000. Avoidable interest is $75,000. Actual interest is $140,000. Capitalize the lower, $75,000, and expense the rest.

scenes.heading: Recording
scenes.say: Bluestem adds $75,000 to the building and expenses $65,000 of interest.

scenes.q: Avoidable interest $90,000; actual interest $70,000. Interest capitalized?
scenes.say: Quick check. Avoidable interest ninety thousand; actual interest seventy thousand. Interest capitalized? Pause and pick.
scenes.reveal: It's B, $70,000: never more than actual interest.

videos.title: Lump-sum and other acquisitions
videos.take: Allocate lump-sum prices by relative fair value; use fair value for stock issued and present value for deferred payments

scenes.say: Bluestem buys a small competitor's plant in Redwood Falls: land, building and equipment, for one price of $1.2 million.

scenes.heading: Relative fair value allocation
scenes.say: Total fair value is $1.5 million, but Bluestem paid $1.2 million, eighty percent. Allocate the price by relative fair value: land $320,000, building $640,000, equipment $240,000. The split matters because land isn't depreciated.

scenes.heading: Other ways to acquire assets
items: Issuing stock: fair value of stock or asset
scenes.say: Other acquisitions: assets bought with deferred payments are recorded at present value, as in Lecture 6. Assets bought with stock are recorded at the fair value of the stock or the asset, whichever is clearer. Donated assets are recorded at fair value with revenue.

scenes.heading: Land acquired for stock
rows: Paid-in capital in excess of par
scenes.say: If Bluestem issued 10,000 shares worth $18 each for a lot, it would record land at $180,000, with $10,000 of common stock at par and $170,000 of paid-in capital.
Notice: the seller's book value never matters. Bluestem records what it gave up or received, at fair value.

scenes.q: Price $900,000; fair values: land $300,000, building $700,000. Building's cost?
scenes.say: Quick check. Price nine hundred thousand; fair values: land three hundred thousand, building seven hundred thousand. Building's cost? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Exchanges of nonmonetary assets
videos.take: With commercial substance, record the new asset at fair value and recognize gains; without it, defer gains

scenes.say: Bluestem trades in an old delivery van and pays $30,000 cash for a new one.

scenes.heading: The old van
scenes.say: The old van cost $40,000 and has $28,000 of accumulated depreciation, a book value of $12,000. The dealer values it at $15,000. That's a $3,000 gain.

sub: as a result of the exchange
scenes.say: Does the exchange have commercial substance? That is, will Bluestem's future cash flows change because of it? A newer, bigger van with lower running costs does change them.

scenes.heading: With commercial substance
scenes.say: With commercial substance, the new van is recorded at fair value given up, $15,000 plus $30,000 cash, or $45,000. The old van and its accumulated depreciation are removed, and the $3,000 gain is recognized.
Without commercial substance, the gain is deferred: the new asset is recorded at the old book value plus cash, $42,000. Losses are always recognized immediately.

scenes.q: Old asset book value $20,000, fair value $16,000, plus $50,000 cash. New asset cost (commercial substance)?
scenes.say: Quick check. Old asset book value twenty thousand, fair value sixteen thousand, plus fifty thousand cash. New asset cost, with commercial substance? Pause and pick.

videos.title: Costs after acquisition
videos.take: Capitalize costs that extend life or improve capacity; expense ordinary repairs

scenes.say: Five years later, the paddle-molding machine needs work. Expense or capitalize?

scenes.big: Capitalize if it adds future benefit
scenes.say: Costs after acquisition are capitalized if they provide future benefits: a longer life, more capacity, better quality output or lower operating costs. Otherwise, they're expensed.

scenes.heading: Examples
rows: New wing added to the warehouse
scenes.say: Ordinary repairs are expensed. An addition, like a new warehouse wing, is capitalized. A major replacement, like a new mold heater, is capitalized, and the old part's cost removed. Rearranging the floor is usually expensed unless material and beneficial for several years.

scenes.heading: Replacing the heater
scenes.say: The new heater costs $32,000. The old one cost $20,000 with $15,000 of depreciation. Bluestem removes it, recognizes a $5,000 loss, and capitalizes the new heater.
Remember Bluestem's $2,500 capitalization threshold from Lecture 2: small items are expensed regardless.

scenes.q: An overhaul extends a machine's life by 4 years. Its cost is:
scenes.say: Quick check. An overhaul extends a machine's life by four years. How is its cost treated? Pause and pick.

warmup: Bluestem pays $250,000 for a machine and $25,000 more to ship, install and test it. Should the $25,000 be expensed this year? Why or why not?
Costs to get the asset ready are part of its cost and benefit future periods.

Expense; capitalize; capitalize (remove old); expense; capitalize.
case: Bluestem paid $1,200,000 for a competitor's plant (land FV $400,000, building FV $800,000, equipment FV $300,000), paid $20,000 legal fees for the whole purchase, $45,000 to rewire the building before use, and $8,000 to repair machines damaged when movers dropped them. The founder wants to allocate more of the price to land 'because it holds value'.
Allocate the price and legal fees.
Treat the rewiring and the repair.
What's wrong with the founder's suggestion, and how does it affect income?

Total cost 1,220,000 allocated by relative fair value: land 325,333, building 650,667, equipment 244,000 (by relative FV). Rewiring capitalized to building (+45,000 = 695,667); repair expensed. Allocating more to land reduces depreciation and overstates income: not allowed; must use relative fair values.

Qualifying assets, during construction, while expenditures and interest are incurred; WAAE × specific rate then weighted-average rate on other debt; limit to actual interest.

With: new van 45,000, gain 3,000. Without: new van 42,000, no gain.
